newsitem.title: ITALY: FAO chief optimistic on eve of World Food Summit.
newsitem.headline: FAO chief optimistic on eve of World Food Summit.

text.p: The head of the U.N.'s food agency said on Tuesday he was confident that this week's World Food Summit would strengthen the fight against hunger and defended its platform from scepticism that action will not follow words.

U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation director general Jacques Diouf spoke on the eve of the summit, at which leaders will pledge to reduce the number of people suffering chronic hunger or malnutrition to half the current 840 million by 2015.
"We have set targets that are more reasonable and more achievable," Diouf said, referring to a ministerial World Food Conference in 1974 which pledged to end hunger within 10 years.
"We are not saying that there will be no person hungry, which is naturally ideal, but we are saying that if we could halve the number of the hungry people we would have already made progress.
"The other element is that this time we have asked those who may make a difference...the leaders of the world, to come themselves," Diouf told Reuters in an interview.

He said their presence would ensure an inter-ministerial approach to food security and that broad non-governmental involvement in summit preparations would mean a partnership in the fight to feed the world.
"Because of all those elements we think that we have a great chance of success provided that the commitments made here are adhered to," Diouf, who is from Senegal, said.
The five-day summit, taking place at FAO's Rome headquarters to cut costs, will be the first gathering of its kind and will open on Wednesday with an address by Pope John Paul.

Guarded by the largest single peacetime security operation in Italy, it is expected to bring together around 100 of heads of state and government, according to FAO, including Cuban President Fidel Castro.

Several non-government development activists have criticised the two summit documents, a Declaration on World Food Security and a Plan of Action that were agreed in advance of the meeting, as bland or utopian statements that will come to nothing.

"There are some very nice things written in the Declaration but it's wishful thinking," said Viplab Halin of the Calcutta Institute for Motivating Self-Employment, one of some 1,000 non-governmental organisations (NGO) also meeting in Rome.

The NGO forum on Tuesday drafted its own statement for the summit, criticising big-business farming and accusing rich countries of contributing to poverty and lack of self-reliance in the Third World by dumping cheap food on their markets.

"We propose a model of economic decentralisation that challenges the current model, which has produced a concentration of wealth and power that now threatens global food security," the NGO draft statement reads.

Asked about criticism of the documents, which contain compromise language on key issues such as trade, population and the role of women, Diouf said any intergovernmental organisation like FAO had to achieve consensus.
"Naturally, in a consensus document you will never find 100 percent of what you want and what your views are but we believe that the document offers a good basis for starting," Diouf said.

The idea for the summit, first proposed by Diouf, was unanimously endorsed by the U.N. General Assembly, although only two of the world's richest nations, the Group of Seven countries, will be sending their prime ministers.

The summit will not seek hard cash pledges and is not scheduled to discuss answers to immediate crises, including the catastrophe in eastern Zaire where more than one million refugees from Rwanda and Burundi are at risk from fighting.
Diouf said the international community should prevent crises by offering countries political and economic support to provide basic necessities, rather than focus only on crisis management.
"If you do not create those conditions the people will fight for the little that is available and the crisis like Zaire we will have in other parts of the world," Diouf said.
"If we just were able to provide those resources ahead of crises, for preventing crises, then I think this world would be in better shape."
